nameStory: Many-flowered Leskea gets its name from the numerous tiny sporophytes (spore capsules) it produces when reproducing. The genus name Pylaisia honors Augustin Pyramus de Candolle's student B.F. Pylaie, a French botanist who collected mosses in North America in the early 1800s.
description: Many-flowered Leskea is a small, mat-forming moss that creates thin, spreading carpets on tree bark. It grows in flattened patches that hug tightly to its surface, rarely more than a few millimeters thick. The moss appears as a delicate, feathery covering that can spread several inches across, with tiny overlapping leaves that give it a scale-like appearance. When dry, it lies completely flat against the bark, but swells slightly when moistened.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thin, flat mats that press tightly against tree bark like green paint, never forming cushions or standing upright

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny overlapping leaves arranged in neat rows, each leaf oval-shaped with a pointed tip, creating a shingle-like pattern visible with a hand lens

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels papery and smooth when dry, becoming slightly spongy when wet, with no bristly or fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright yellowish-green when moist, fading to dull brownish-green or golden when dry, never deep forest green

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on smooth bark of deciduous trees, particularly preferring ash, maple, and basswood trunks

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces many small, reddish-brown capsules on short stalks that emerge perpendicular to the bark surface in spring

habitat: Many-flowered Leskea grows on the bark of deciduous trees in moist woodlands throughout New England, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like ash, maple, basswood, and occasionally oak. It prefers the lower trunks and larger branches of mature trees in areas with good air circulation but protection from direct sunlight. You'll most often find it in rich, mesic forests at low to moderate elevations, rarely above 2000 feet.

seasonality.spring: Most visible season as sporophytes develop, appearing as tiny reddish capsules on short stalks. The moss is bright green and fully hydrated from spring rains, making identification easiest.
seasonality.summer: Remains present but may appear brownish and flattened against bark during dry periods. Look for it on the shadier, north-facing sides of trees where it retains more moisture.
seasonality.fall: Sporophytes have usually shed their spores by now, but the moss itself remains visible, often taking on golden-brown tones as temperatures cool and humidity increases.
seasonality.winter: Still present but appears most compressed and brown. Can be revived with a spray bottle to see its true green color and growth form.

funFact: This tiny moss can completely dehydrate and appear dead for months, but within minutes of rain touching it, it springs back to life and begins photosynthesis again—a superpower that allows it to survive in the challenging environment of tree bark where water comes and goes unpredictably.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bark-dwelling mosses like Entodon or Platygyrium, but Many-flowered Leskea's combination of extremely flat growth, yellowish-green color, and preference for smooth deciduous bark helps distinguish it. Remember: if it's puffy or grows on rough bark or rocks, it's probably something else.
compareHints: Many-flowered Leskea differs from its close relative Pylaisia selwynii primarily in leaf shape and sporophyte abundance—selwynii has more elongated leaves and produces fewer capsules. However, selwynii is much rarer in New England, making Many-flowered Leskea the more likely find. Both species share the characteristic flat, mat-forming growth on deciduous tree bark.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Many-flowered Leskea (the other Pylaisia in our region), Selwyn's Pylaisia forms much thinner, more delicate mats with a more pronounced silky texture and golden sheen when dry.
